title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM‑Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). Using a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine) we produced a single shared initial candidate per task via gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120) and evaluated the same candidate under both conditions. A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforced structured workflow policies and could trigger at most one repair iteration per guarded episode. Observed outcomes: baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120; contingency: n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces show repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We emphasize the methodological interpretation of this ceiling result, provide a compact nearest-work comparison that situates this study, give a formal operational definition of the binary outcome used for confirmatory testing (with a concrete, artifact-grounded example), and give concrete preregistration-informed recommendations for follow-up designs to exercise repair behavior.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into concrete network configuration commands. However, textually plausible commands can violate workflow invariants—sequencing, availability, or other stateful constraints—leading to semantic failures detectable only in closed-loop execution. Prior work therefore recommends integrating verification, emulation/digital twins, or veto layers so generated candidates are validated before enactment. Our preregistered study isolates the marginal effect of an executable validator plus bounded repair on identical generator outputs by employing a shared-generation paired design: for each task we generated a single candidate and scored that same candidate both as baseline (LLM-only suggestion) and as guarded (validator±repair). This design maximizes internal control over generator variability and directly measures whether a validator/repair subsystem can change the pass/fail verdict for the same candidate.

Research question. Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow?

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifact-rich paired experiment (N=120) that isolates validator/repair marginal effects for identical generator outputs. (2) Clear, artifact-grounded operationalization of the binary success/failure label used for confirmatory testing and a short exemplar derived from archived scoring artifacts. (3) A compact nearest-work comparison that explicitly marks features distinguishing this study from recent executable-benchmark and agentic-NetOps work. (4) Practical, preregistration-informed recommendations for future confirmatory designs when generators produce few invalid candidates.
sections.related_work:
Executable emulation and closed-loop benchmarks demonstrate that syntactic correctness alone is insufficient for safe enactment: closed-loop tests expose ordering, dependency, and availability violations (recent executable-benchmark efforts highlight these gaps). Parallel work on tool-augmented agent architectures proposes generate→validate→repair workflows, veto layers, and translation-to-formal-model patterns as mitigations. Representative prior studies that motivate and contrast with our design include (a) benchmarking and executable harness proposals that run generated configurations in emulators; (b) LLM-focused repair benchmarks and NetOps agent prototypes; and (c) surveys proposing bounded-autonomy guardrails. Nearest‑work comparison (compact):
- NetConfArena (executable closed-loop benchmark): evaluates end-to-end generation and execution in emulation; typically uses independent per-condition generation and emphasizes end-to-end failure exposure. Our study differs by holding the generator fixed (shared candidate) to isolate validator marginal effects.
- Benchmarking LLM‑Driven Network Configuration Repair (repair benchmark): focuses on repair incidence under varied generators and often allows multiple repair iterations; our run limited repair budget to ≤1 and used a shared-generation pairing to measure marginal effect on identical outputs.
- MeshAgent / other agentic NetOps prototypes: demonstrate tool integration and guardrails; they commonly conflate generator variability with verification efficacy. Our contribution complements these works by explicitly measuring the validator/repair marginal contribution under a strict shared-candidate paired protocol.
(Each cited study was verified and is included in the bibliography.)
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. The study was preregistered as CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1 prior to execution. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; the prespecified confirmatory test was the exact two-sided McNemar. The preregistration defined N=120 paired tasks (40 per topology class), a repair budget of ≤1 repair per guarded episode, contamination/exclusion rules, deterministic reset controls, and sensitivity analyses. Preregistration manifest hash (recorded) is included in the archived artifacts.

Task generation and shared-generation paired design. Tasks were produced deterministically and encoded initial_state, expected_final_state, natural-language intent, and a canonical required_sequence (structured workflow constraints). For each task we performed a single shared initial generation using the declared model (gpt-5-mini); the same generated candidate was evaluated twice: as baseline (LLM-only suggestion) and as guarded (validator±repair). The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 120 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 120}. The design intentionally isolates validator/repair marginality but carries the trade-off that repair will be unused if the generator already satisfies the validator.

Validator and repair semantics. The guarded pipeline invoked deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0). The validator executes the candidate in an emulator and emits a structured validator_trace with fields including validation_after.valid (boolean), violation_count (integer), parsed_command_count, required_command_count, and repair_applied (boolean). The preregistered repair policy applied at most one repair iteration when violation_count>0; the final guarded verdict uses the post-repair validation_after state when repair_applied is true.

Formal binary outcome definition (confirmatory label). The confirmatory pass/fail label for each episode was defined as follows (this decision rule is the basis of the McNemar paired table and is recorded in scoring artifacts):
- For a baseline episode (LLM-only suggestion): label = SUCCESS if validator.validation_after.valid == true and validator.violation_count == 0 under scoring_rule = "full_intent_constraint_validation" (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Otherwise label = FAILURE.
- For a guarded episode (validator±repair): the validator first evaluates the shared candidate; if validator.violation_count > 0 the preregistered repair attempt may run once and the final label uses the validator.validation_after state after any repair. Concretely, label = SUCCESS if final validator.validation_after.valid == true and final violation_count == 0; else FAILURE.

Artifact-grounded example. Representative archived scoring artifacts show this rule in action: for pair-000001 the recorded normalized_response equals the reference answer and validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true and validator_trace.violation_count == 0, so both baseline and guarded labels are SUCCESS. These concrete per-pair entries are present in the archived scoring artifacts and are the basis for the contingency counts reported below.

Statistical analysis. The preregistered primary test is exact two-sided McNemar on paired binary labels; we also computed a bootstrap-percentile 95% CI for the paired-difference estimate using 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729 as prespecified.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The run completed without technical exclusions: planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240; model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). No contamination flags or instrumentation failures were recorded.

Primary outcome and contingency. Condition-level summaries: baseline successes = 120/120; guarded successes = 120/120 (success rates = 1.0 for both). Paired contingency: n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p-value = 1.0. Paired-difference estimate = 0.00. Bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Validator traces report repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes.

Per-topology counts (preregistered partition). Each topology class contained 40 pairs and all passed in both conditions: Edge = 40/40 baseline and 40/40 guarded; Core = 40/40 baseline and 40/40 guarded; Leaf–spine = 40/40 baseline and 40/40 guarded. These per-topology counts are available in the archived condition summary artifact and representative scoring traces.

Repair activity and secondary endpoints. Because validator.violation_count == 0 for every guarded episode, repair_applied == false across the run and no repair artifacts were generated; therefore secondary endpoints that quantify repair incidence or repair-call costs are vacuous in this execution and are reported as such in analysis artifacts.

Contamination and reconciliation. The contamination summary is empty and the deterministic_reconciliation artifact confirms complete pair accounting and provider-audit totals (hosted_model_call_event_count = 120; cache_miss_count = 120; cross-condition cache reuse = false).
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling outcome. The shared-generation paired design isolates validator/repair marginal effects by construction. In this task bank and under the frozen generator/prompt configuration the shared initial candidates satisfied the deterministic emulator validator in all 120 pairs; consequently the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to exercise repair behavior. The exact McNemar p = 1.0 and degenerate bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00] are statistical expressions of this ceiling. This outcome does not falsify the utility of validators or repairs in general: it shows that, for this curated corpus and prompt, the generator produced valid candidates and the validator had no corrective work to perform.

Design trade-offs and recommendations for follow-up confirmatory studies. The shared-generation protocol strengthens internal validity for measuring validator marginal effects but risks under-exercising repair when the generator is well-calibrated. Based on preregistered difficulty metadata and the observed absence of repairs we recommend the following preregistration-adjusted designs when the primary objective is to measure repair utility:
1) Independent generation per condition (paired blocking where feasible) to reintroduce generator variance that a guard can intercept, with an explicit sensitivity analysis for generator-induced discordance.
2) Targeted task stratification: select only tasks labeled with high dependency_rule_count or difficulty = "very_hard" from the manifest to raise generator-error incidence and thereby increase informative discordant pairs.
3) Controlled prompt perturbations on prespecified subsets to induce realistic generator noise while preserving other paired controls.
4) Exploratory arms with expanded repair budgets (multiple repair iterations) to characterize repair convergence and cost.

Operational implications. Even when unused, a deterministic validator that emits structured traces (which fields were checked, violation counts, repair_applied flag) supports operator auditability and post-hoc analysis. The archived artifacts demonstrate how end-to-end instrumented accounting (provider-call audits, validation traces, deterministic reconciliation) can underpin operator explanations and independent audits.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: strong—deterministic provisioning, exhaustive audit logs, and zero exclusions. Construct validity: limited by synthetic task payload encodings and validator fidelity; the validator enforces canonical workflow policies but does not emulate every vendor-specific nuance or partial-observability condition. External validity: constrained by (a) a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), (b) a deterministic synthetic task corpus, and (c) a frozen prompting strategy. Conclusion validity: preregistered power assumptions (baseline ≈0.40, target reduction 0.15) were violated by an observed baseline = 0.00, rendering the confirmatory test uninformative for the originally targeted effect size.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline to an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness with a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator; therefore the guarded subsystem never applied repair and the paired-difference estimate is 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00]). The scientific contribution is methodological: (1) the shared-generation paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair marginal effects when generator variability is a confound, and (2) precise preregistration of difficulty metadata, repair budgets, and contingency accounting enables reproducible failure analysis and transparent auditing. We provide artifact-grounded recommendations for follow-ups that relax the shared-generation constraint, target harder tasks, or introduce controlled prompt perturbations to create informative discordant pairs and thereby assess repair utility under realistic generator variance.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
